title: Readout and Multiplexing
intro: A quantum reservoir is only as good as the features its readout extracts: which observables are measured, how many times per input, from how many reservoirs, and with how many shots. This page sets out the options and their costs, with simulations.

blocks.text: Any Hermitian $O$ gives a feature $\operatorname{Tr}(O\rho_k)$, but each measurement setting (a choice of basis per qubit) costs its own shots. In the computational basis one setting gives a bitstring per shot, and from those bitstrings every diagonal observable can be estimated at once: all $2^n-1$ Z-strings $Z_{i}$, $Z_iZ_j$, $Z_iZ_jZ_l$, and so on. Off-diagonal observables need other settings (rotate before measuring), multiplying the shot cost.

items: Local magnetisations $\langle Z_i\rangle$: $n$ features, lowest variance, standard choice.
Two-point correlators $\langle Z_iZ_j\rangle$: $n(n-1)/2$ more features from the same shots; they add quadratic information about the state.

Higher Z-strings: up to $2^n-1$ from the same shots, but a weight-$w$ string in a scrambled state is typically small and costs as many shots to resolve as any other, so in practice only low weights are used.
Other bases: $\langle X_i\rangle$ or full local tomography multiply settings by up to $3^n$ (all Pauli bases).

blocks.text: Split the evolution between inputs into $V$ sub-steps and read after each: $x_k = (\langle O\rangle_{k,1},\dots,\langle O\rangle_{k,V})$. The features at different sub-times are different linear functionals of the same state (the Heisenberg-evolved observables $U^{\dagger v}OU^{v}$), so for generic dynamics they are linearly independent until their number approaches the dimension of the reachable operator space. Cost: $V$ times more readouts per input, and on a single device each one is a separate experiment (or a weak measurement; see Online Protocols (#/qrc/hardware/online-protocols)).

Nakajima and coauthors proposed running several small reservoirs with different random couplings in parallel, all driven by the same input, and concatenating their features. $K$ reservoirs of $n$ qubits give $K$ times the features while each stays small enough to control and to simulate classically; the price is that information never mixes between them, so a $K\times n$ system is not as rich as one $Kn$-qubit reservoir could be in principle. Nakajima et al. showed numerically on benchmark tasks that this boosts performance well beyond that of a single small reservoir, and examined where the technique stops paying off.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from itertools import combinations

X = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]], complex); Z = np.diag([1, -1]).astype(complex)
def op(o, i, n):
    m = np.array([[1]], complex)
    for k in range(n): m = np.kron(m, o if k == i else np.eye(2))
    return m
n, D = 4, 16
zd = [np.real(np.diag(op(Z, i, n))) for i in range(n)]
zz = [zd[i] * zd[j] for i, j in combinations(range(n), 2)]       # diagonal of Z_i Z_j

def reservoir(seed, dt, V):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    H = sum(rng.uniform(-0.5, 0.5) * op(X, i, n) @ op(X, j, n) for i in range(n) for j in range(i + 1, n))
    H = H + sum(op(Z, i, n) for i in range(n))
    E, P = np.linalg.eigh(H)
    return P @ np.diag(np.exp(-1j * E * dt / V)) @ P.conj().T

def run(s, U, V, corr):
    rho = np.eye(D) / D; out = []
    for x in s:
        r4 = rho.reshape(2, 8, 2, 8); rest = r4[0, :, 0, :] + r4[1, :, 1, :]
        psi = np.array([np.sqrt(1 - x), np.sqrt(x)]); rho = np.kron(np.outer(psi, psi), rest); f = []
        for _ in range(V):
            rho = U @ rho @ U.conj().T; d = np.real(np.diag(rho))
            f += [z @ d for z in zd] + ([z @ d for z in zz] if corr else [])
        out.append(f)
    return np.array(out)

def narma2(u):
    y = np.zeros_like(u)
    for t in range(2, len(u)): y[t] = 0.4 * y[t-1] + 0.4 * y[t-1] * y[t-2] + 0.6 * u[t-1] ** 3 + 0.1
    return y

s = np.random.default_rng(101).uniform(0, 1, 1400); yN = narma2(s / 2)
wash, tr = 200, 800
def fit(F, y, lam=1e-7):
    F = np.hstack([F, np.ones((len(F), 1))]); A = F[wash:wash + tr]
    w = np.linalg.solve(A.T @ A + lam * np.eye(A.shape[1]), A.T @ y[wash:wash + tr])
    return F[wash + tr:] @ w, y[wash + tr:]
def scores(F):
    mc = 0
    for d in range(1, 13):
        p, t = fit(F, np.roll(s, d)); mc += np.corrcoef(p, t)[0, 1] ** 2
    p, t = fit(F, yN)
    return mc, np.mean((p - t) ** 2) / np.var(t)

cases = [("<Z_i>, V=1", lambda: run(s, reservoir(1, 10, 1), 1, False)),
         ("<Z_i>, V=5", lambda: run(s, reservoir(1, 10, 5), 5, False)),
         ("<Z_i>+<Z_iZ_j>, V=1", lambda: run(s, reservoir(1, 10, 1), 1, True)),
         ("<Z_i>+<Z_iZ_j>, V=5", lambda: run(s, reservoir(1, 10, 5), 5, True)),
         ("2 reservoirs x <Z_i>, V=5", lambda: np.hstack([run(s, reservoir(1, 10, 5), 5, False),
                                                          run(s, reservoir(2, 10, 5), 5, False)]))]
for name, f in cases:
    F = f(); mc, nm = scores(F)
    print(f"{name:28s} features={F.shape[1]:3d}  MC={mc:.2f}  NARMA2 NMSE={nm:.3f}")

blocks.text: Same 4-qubit reservoir ($h=1$, $\Delta t=10$), scored on memory capacity (delays 1 to 12) and NARMA2 test NMSE:

items: $\langle Z_i\rangle$ and $\langle Z_iZ_j\rangle$, $V=1$: 10 features, MC 2.82, NMSE 0.143.
$\langle Z_i\rangle$ and $\langle Z_iZ_j\rangle$, $V=5$: 50 features, MC 5.48, NMSE 0.066.
Two independent reservoirs, $\langle Z_i\rangle$, $V=5$: 40 features, MC 5.30, NMSE 0.067.

blocks.text: Correlators are the cheapest upgrade: from the same bitstrings, 10 features at $V=1$ do about as well on NARMA2 as 20 virtual-node features. Spatial multiplexing and correlators with virtual nodes land at the same place, around 0.07, for very different hardware costs.

With $V=5$ and exact expectations MC is about 5.1. Now raise shots from 0: at 100 000 the curve is nearly unchanged, at 1000 MC drops to about 3.3, at 100 to about 1.9. The long-delay terms go first, because they are small linear combinations buried under noise.

blocks.caption: Each shot gives z = ±1; the estimate of <Z> from S shots.

blocks.text: With $M$ features per input, $T$ inputs and $S$ shots per feature, a naive single-device experiment needs about $S\,T$ runs if every feature of a step comes from the same shots (all Z-strings at once), times $V$ if the virtual nodes must be separate experiments, and more if the reservoir must be re-run from the start to reach step $k$ (the restart cost discussed in Measurement Back-Action (#/qrc/hardware/measurement-back-action)). Ridge regularisation helps: with noisy features, the optimal $\lambda$ grows roughly with the noise variance, which shrinks weights on weak, noisy directions.

items: Standardise features before ridge; their scales differ by orders of magnitude between local and high-weight observables.

A polynomial or kernel readout on the features adds nonlinearity classically. It can raise accuracy but moves computation out of the quantum system, and makes comparisons with classical reservoirs less clean.
Online training (recursive least squares) suits streams but changes nothing in the feature argument.

blocks.title: Feature count with correlators
blocks.text: A 10-qubit reservoir is read in the computational basis after each of $V=4$ virtual-node steps; the readout uses all $\langle Z_i\rangle$ and $\langle Z_iZ_j\rangle$. How many features per input?
solution: Per input: $55\times4 = 220$, all from the same bitstrings at each sub-step.

blocks.title: Shots for a target precision
blocks.text: A feature with $\langle Z\rangle \approx 0$ is estimated from 1000 shots. What is its standard error, and how many shots would bring it to 0.001?
solution: For 0.001: $S = 1/0.001^2 = 10^6$ shots, a thousand times more for about 30 times the precision.

blocks.title: Correlators or virtual nodes
blocks.text: From the table, which costs fewer distinct measurement times per input to reach NARMA2 NMSE near 0.14: virtual nodes with $\langle Z_i\rangle$ or correlators at $V=1$?
solution: $\langle Z_i\rangle$ with $V=5$ gives 0.138 using 5 readout times per input.
$\langle Z_i\rangle+\langle Z_iZ_j\rangle$ with $V=1$ gives 0.143 using 1 readout time, since correlators come from the same bitstrings.
Correlators at $V=1$: five times fewer readouts for the same error.
